what_it_does: When a large language model processes a long conversation or document, it must remember every word it has already seen. It does this using a key-value cache (KV cache) — essentially a running notepad stored in memory that grows with each new word and can consume tens of gigabytes for sequences of tens of thousands of words. Many recent systems try to shrink this notepad by permanently deleting entries for words deemed unimportant, but that can hurt accuracy if those words turn out to matter later. ClusterKV instead groups the notepad entries by meaning (semantic clustering — putting entries about similar topics into the same bucket) and keeps only the most relevant buckets active at any time, bringing the rest back from slower storage on demand. This lets the model keep a small active notepad budget (roughly 1,000–2,000 entries) while still being able to recall information from 32,000-word contexts, reportedly matching full-cache quality without permanent loss.
